# EDA using ggpairs {#sec-eda-ggpairs}













`eda-gwalkr.qmd` left you with a question rather than an answer, and I did that on purpose: *which of these variables are quietly telling me the same story twice?* You'd already felt the shape of that question coming. Back in @sec-eda-ggplot, we zoomed in on exactly one pair (GFAP intensity against PDGFR-β intensity) and built an interactive scatter plot just to look at how those two markers move together across DPI. That was deliberate and it was informative: we saw the relationship strengthen and spread out as the tissue moves further from the ischemic event. But it was also, by construction, one pair out of many possible pairs. `cell_data` has five numeric columns in the subset we've been using. Two of them is a scatter plot. Five of them is ten scatter plots, and nobody sits down and builds ten `ggiraph` objects by hand just to satisfy a hunch.

This chapter is about answering that GWalkR question properly: not by dragging variables around a widget, but by looking at every pair of variables in `cell_data` at once, deliberately, the way EDA is supposed to work.

## Why look at all pairs at once?

Here's an everyday version of the problem. Imagine you're triaging a stack of grant applications and you suspect two reviewers on your panel always give nearly identical scores (not because they coordinated, but because they're weighing the same criteria in their heads). Checking that suspicion one reviewer-pair at a time, by pulling out two scoresheets and eyeballing them, works fine if you have three reviewers. It falls apart with fifteen. What you actually want is one table that shows you, at a glance, how correlated *every* pair of reviewers is with every other pair, so the redundant ones jump out instead of you having to go looking for them.

That table, applied to data instead of grant reviewers, is what a [correlation matrix]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} gives you: a grid where every variable in your dataset is compared against every other variable at once, instead of one deliberately chosen pair at a time. It's the natural generalization of the single scatter plot from @sec-eda-ggplot: same idea, scaled up from "one relationship I already suspected" to "every relationship I haven't checked yet."

Why does this matter before you've fit a single model? Because two variables that are almost interchangeable (one that tells you almost nothing the other one doesn't already tell you) are a problem you want to catch in the exploration stage, not discover three chapters from now when a regression model hands you coefficients that make no sense. This chapter isn't about diagnosing an already-fitted model (that's a narrower, later question we'll pick back up in @sec-linear-regression-assumptions, once there's an actual model on the table to interrogate). Right now we're just asking the more general question: of the variables sitting in front of us, which ones are quietly duplicating each other?

Let's load the data we've been building intuition about since the start of this part, and get looking.






::: {#tbl-cell_data_ggpairs_tbl .cell tbl-cap='Cell data table used for pairwise covariance exploration'}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(here)
library(gt)

cell_data <- read.csv(here("project/AnalysisData/Cells_Gfap-Pdgfrb.csv"))

gt(head(cell_data))
```

As we've done before, let's subset down to the numeric measurements we actually care about comparing, so the matrix we're about to build stays readable instead of drowning in identifier columns:






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cell_data_sub <- subset(cell_data, select = c(Tissue_Area, Pdgfrb_Area, Pdgfrb_IntDen, Gfap_Area, Gfap_IntDen))
```
:::






## The full picture with `ggpairs`

A single scatter plot answers one question at a time. What we want here is closer to a contact sheet: every pairwise scatter plot laid out in a grid at once, plus the correlation coefficient for each pair, plus each variable's own distribution along the diagonal, all in one figure. That's exactly what `ggpairs()` from the [GGally](https://ggobi.github.io/ggally/reference/ggpairs.html) package [@ggally] builds for you; it's the tool of choice here precisely because it refuses to make you choose which pair to look at first; it shows you all of them and lets the data tell you where to look.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(GGally)

ggpairs(cell_data_sub)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Correlation between predictor variables in the `cell_data` frame.](eda-ggpairs_files/figure-pdf/fig-cell_data_ggpairs-1.pdf){#fig-cell_data_ggpairs}
:::
:::






For more plotting options, refer to the [GGally](https://ggobi.github.io/ggally/reference/ggpairs.html) documentation. Here, @fig-cell_data_ggpairs earns its keep immediately.

Look at the `Corr` values in the upper triangle: Pdgfrb_Area and Pdgfrb_IntDen sit at 0.94, and Gfap_Area and Gfap_IntDen sit at 0.98. Both pairs are, for practical purposes, telling us the same thing twice. If you know the area a marker covers, you already know almost everything you'd have learned from its integrated density; the two aren't independent pieces of biological information, they're two ways of measuring almost the same underlying signal. That's the exact redundancy GWalkR's closing question was pointing you toward, now stated precisely instead of suspected.

::: callout-tip
A correlation this high between two predictors doesn't mean either variable is wrong or useless on its own; it means that, together, they carry a lot less independent information than two separate columns in a spreadsheet might suggest. Worth remembering the next time you're tempted to throw every column you measured into a model "just to be safe."
:::

## Two other views of the same idea: `corrplot` and `heatmap`

`ggpairs()` is thorough, but a full matrix of scatter plots and histograms is a lot to put in front of a labmate or a manuscript reviewer when all you actually want to communicate is *which pairs are correlated, and how strongly*. For that narrower job, a plain correlation matrix visualized as color is often the more honest, and more readable, choice, so let's build the same underlying comparison two more ways.

First, `corrplot` [@corrplot]. We start from `cor()`, base R's own correlation function, and hand the resulting matrix to `corrplot()` to turn into color:






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(corrplot)

cell_data_sub_matrix <- cor(cell_data_sub)
corrplot(cell_data_sub_matrix, type = "upper", order = "hclust",
         tl.col = "black", tl.srt = 45)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Correlation matrix for predictor variables in the `cell_data` frame.](eda-ggpairs_files/figure-pdf/fig-cell_data_corrplot-1.pdf){#fig-cell_data_corrplot}
:::
:::






@fig-cell_data_corrplot shows the same story as the `ggpairs` grid, distilled down to circle size and color: the darkest, largest circles off the diagonal are exactly the Pdgfrb_Area/Pdgfrb_IntDen and Gfap_Area/Gfap_IntDen pairs we already flagged. The `hclust` ordering is doing a bit of extra work for you here too: it groups correlated variables next to each other automatically, so redundant clusters show up as solid blocks rather than being scattered across the grid.

Some researchers prefer a heatmap for the same underlying matrix: a matter of taste and audience more than statistics:






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
heatmap(x = cell_data_sub_matrix, col = hcl.colors(20, "viridis"), symm = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Heatmap for predictor variables in the `cell_data` frame.](eda-ggpairs_files/figure-pdf/fig-cell_data_heatmap-1.pdf){#fig-cell_data_heatmap}
:::
:::






@fig-cell_data_heatmap clusters the same two redundant pairs together along both axes, using color intensity in place of `corrplot`'s circles. Three plots, one finding, which is itself worth noticing. When three different visualizations of the same matrix all point at the same two pairs, that's not a coincidence of plotting choices; it's the data being genuinely unambiguous about where the redundancy lives.

## What this does (and doesn't) tell us

A correlation matrix, in any of the three forms above, tells you *which* variables move together. It does not, by itself, tell you what to do about it, and that's an honest limitation, not an oversight. Whether Pdgfrb_Area and Pdgfrb_IntDen being nearly redundant actually matters depends entirely on what you do next: if you're just describing the dataset, it's a fact worth noting and moving on from. If you're about to fit a regression model with both of them as predictors, it's a warning sign that deserves a second look, one that, once we're standing in front of an actual fitted model, has its own name (multicollinearity) and its own diagnostic (the variance inflation factor) in @sec-linear-regression-assumptions.

For now, keep the finding, not the machinery: `Pdgfrb_Area`/`Pdgfrb_IntDen` and `Gfap_Area`/`Gfap_IntDen` are each carrying largely overlapping information. That's one more entry on the running list of things we now know about `cell_data`, a list the next chapter will pull all the way together before we let this dataset anywhere near a model.
